title: The Courtroom Escape Hatches Sovereign Citizens Swear By

notes: s56: dropped "only" and named both gaps the record has (unreported hearings, per s54, and no US-wide count), as the reviewer suggested. The rare apparent wins (Credit River 1968, Porisky 2000, Naudi) stay out: those passages are not cited in the package and adding them needs record-sources.

sentences.text: Picture an Ohio courtroom, and a man facing four criminal charges from a run-in with police at the end of 2023, standing up to read a statement he plainly believed would protect him.

assertions.text: In State v. Smith, the defendant faced four charges arising from an encounter with officers on December 22, 2023, and opened his trial with a prepared statement.

sentences.note: The passage gives the date of the encounter (December 22, 2023) and "all four charges"; it does not name them, so the narration does not either. "criminal" is the reviewer's call: a trial with a plea of not guilty and fines.

sentences.text: He told the court he reserved his "unalienable rights per UCC 1-308 without prejudice", and then he added: "I give the Court no consent".

assertions.text: The defendant in State v. Smith said he reserved his "unalienable rights per UCC 1-308 without prejudice".

quote.text: unalienable rights per UCC 1-308 without prejudice

assertions.text: The defendant in State v. Smith told the court "I give the Court no consent".

quote.text: I give the Court no consent

sentences.text: If you have spent any time in certain corners of YouTube, you know what those words are supposed to do.
They are supposed to switch the court off.
They did not: he was found guilty of all four charges against him and fined for each one, though he was not sent to jail.

assertions.text: Despite reserving rights under UCC 1-308 and withholding consent, the State v. Smith defendant was found guilty of all four charges and fined for each, with no jail time.

sentences.text: So is there anything at all you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's reach?
We will take the popular escape hatches one at a time, read the document each one points to, and see what the courts have said about it.

The belief underneath them is simple: a channel called Out of Babylon tells viewers that "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction".

assertions.text: The Out of Babylon channel says "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction".

quote.text: there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction
quote.speaker: Out of Babylon

sentences.text: Rob Menard, a Canadian freeman-on-the-land figure, claimed in a television interview that Canada's chief justice had said "no one can provide adjudication Services without the consent of both members of the adjudication"; that is his account, not a ruling.

assertions.text: Rob Menard, interviewed as a freeman on the land, attributes to the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada the words "no one can provide adjudication Services without the consent of both members of the adjudication".

quote.text: no one can provide adjudication Services without the consent of both members of the adjudication
quote.speaker: Rob Menard

assertions.text: Netolitzky's history of these movements in Canada names Robert Arthur Menard, a British Columbia street comedian, as the creator of the freeman idea that consent can be withdrawn from government.

sentences.note: The source title is a CBC News broadcast interview; "television interview" rests on that title. The statement context shows Menard attributing the words to the chief justice in a talk; the narration flags that as his claim and does not name her or repeat the unverified details.

sentences.text: From that one idea, that a court needs your consent, the movement has built a whole toolkit.
When you sign something, you are told to add a code section beside your name; The Grown Academy, for example, tells viewers to "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved".

assertions.text: The Grown Academy tells viewers to "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved".

quote.text: write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved
quote.speaker: The Grown Academy

sentences.text: Another channel, Americans In Action, calls UCC 1-308 "a Lifeline for free men and women to uphold the constitution".

assertions.text: Americans In Action says UCC 1-308 is "a Lifeline for free men and women to uphold the constitution".

quote.text: a Lifeline for free men and women to uphold the constitution
quote.speaker: Americans In Action

sentences.text: When you walk into the courtroom, you are told to look at the flag: a letter to the editor printed in the Mountain Democrat newspaper says "The fringe denotes Admiralty law’s jurisdiction".

assertions.text: A letter to the editor printed in the Mountain Democrat says "The fringe denotes Admiralty law’s jurisdiction".

quote.text: The fringe denotes Admiralty law’s jurisdiction
quote.speaker: Mountain Democrat

sentences.text: Behind it all sits a history lesson: the act of 1871, says a channel called SYDLIS, is "exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation".

assertions.text: The SYDLIS channel says the act of 1871 "is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation".

quote.text: exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation
quote.speaker: SYDLIS

sentences.note: The recorded quote reads "that is exactly what changed"; the checked quotation starts at "exactly".

sentences.text: If the government is a company, its laws are company rules: Americans In Action says "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation", and the website jonhoyle.com sums up where that leads: "All law is commerce. All commerce is contract. No contract, no case".

assertions.text: Americans In Action says "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation".

quote.text: these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation
quote.speaker: Americans In Action

assertions.text: The website jonhoyle.com says "All law is commerce. All commerce is contract. No contract, no case".

quote.text: All law is commerce. All commerce is contract. No contract, no case

sentences.text: So that is the toolkit: refuse your consent, reserve your rights under a commercial code, point at the fringe, invoke an old statute, and treat every law as a contract you never signed.
Each trick points at something real. The question is whether the real thing says what the trick needs it to say.
Start with the code section, because you can read it yourself.

UCC 1-308 says that a party who goes ahead and performs "with explicit reservation of rights" does not thereby give up the rights it reserved, and that phrases such as without prejudice or under protest are enough to do it.

assertions.text: UCC 1-308(a): a party that performs, promises performance or assents to performance "with explicit reservation of rights" does not prejudice the rights reserved; words such as without prejudice or under protest are sufficient.

quote.text: with explicit reservation of rights

sentences.text: The official comment explains what that is for: it "provides machinery for the continuation of performance along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute".

assertions.text: The official comment to UCC 1-308 says the section "provides machinery for the continuation of performance along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute".

quote.text: provides machinery for the continuation of performance along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute

sentences.text: Picture a builder who takes delivery of timber she thinks is the wrong grade: she can accept it and pay under protest, keep the job moving, and still argue about the price later.
sentences.note: Plainly hypothetical, no figures; it illustrates the comment's "going ahead with delivery, acceptance, or payment" under protest (ucc L26).

sentences.text: That is the whole job of the section: keeping a contract moving during a dispute. Nothing in its text or comment mentions courts, criminal charges, or consent to a judge's authority.

assertions.text: The text and official comment of UCC 1-308 concern continuing performance of a commercial contract during a dispute and say nothing about courts' jurisdiction or criminal law.

sentences.text: Courts have noticed: in the Ohio case we started with, the appeals court wrote that "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing".

assertions.text: The Ohio appeals court in State v. Smith wrote that "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing".

quote.text: Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing

sentences.text: So the code section is not a shield; it is a tool for business disputes. But what about simply refusing to consent?
In United States v. Benabe, the federal appeals court for the Seventh Circuit dealt with defendants who said their status put them beyond the court's power; the trial court dismissed those arguments.

assertions.text: In United States v. Benabe the Seventh Circuit reviewed defendants who raised immunity arguments based on their claimed status; the trial court properly dismissed them.

sentences.text: The appeals court's answer was blunt: whatever status a person claims, sovereign citizen, secured-party creditor or flesh-and-blood human being, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts".

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit held that whatever status a person claims, be it sovereign citizen, secured-party creditor or flesh-and-blood human being, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts".

quote.text: that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts

sentences.text: It added that such theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented", and it listed its own earlier cases, one of which described a sovereign citizen defense as having "no conceivable validity in American law".

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit said such theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented".

quote.text: should be rejected summarily, however they are presented

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit cited its earlier decision in Schneider describing a sovereign citizen defense as having "no conceivable validity in American law".

quote.text: no conceivable validity in American law

qualifications: The sentence names the court; the broad reviews are Canadian and Australasian, as the qualifications section says.

sentences.text: The same argument turns up on the other side of the world: a review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand describes three consent arguments, one from a man held on a warrant who treated the court's authority as a matter of his consent; all three were unsuccessful.

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre describe three consent-based claimants, one a habeas claimant who treated the court's authority as a matter of his consent; all three were unsuccessful.

sentences.text: The authors put the problem in one line: "no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it, especially for purposes of tax or criminal law".

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre write that "no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it, especially for purposes of tax or criminal law".

quote.text: no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it, especially for purposes of tax or criminal law

sentences.text: Next, the flag.
In McCann v. Greenway, a federal court in Missouri faced the gold-fringe argument and noted that other courts had already called it frivolous, totally frivolous and preposterous.

assertions.text: In McCann v. Greenway the court noted that other courts had labelled the fringe argument frivolous, totally frivolous and preposterous.

sentences.text: Then, "in the interest of killing this argument for good", the judge worked through the law of the flag.

assertions.text: The McCann court examined the law of the flag "in the interest of killing this argument for good".

quote.text: in the interest of killing this argument for good

sentences.text: The flag statute describes stripes and stars, and an Army statement from the 1920s, quoted by the court, said that a fringe "is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance".

assertions.text: The McCann court quoted the Army Adjutant General, from the 1920s, that in flag manufacture a fringe "is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance".

quote.text: is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance

sentences.text: And even if a fringe did mean something, the court said, it could not shrink the court's power, because jurisdiction "is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child’s game".

assertions.text: The McCann court held that fringe has no legal significance and that jurisdiction "is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child’s game".

quote.text: is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child’s game

sentences.text: The Lux Law Firm, which explains these cases online, puts it simply: "There are no cases attributing any kind of legal significance to the fringes on a flag in an American courthouse".

assertions.text: The Lux Law Firm says "There are no cases attributing any kind of legal significance to the fringes on a flag in an American courthouse".

quote.text: There are no cases attributing any kind of legal significance to the fringes on a flag in an American courthouse

sentences.text: Now the history lesson.
In 1871 Congress did pass a law, titled "An act to provide a government for the District of Columbia", the federal district around the capital.

assertions.text: In 1871 Congress passed "An act to provide a government for the District of Columbia".

quote.text: An act to provide a government for the District of Columbia

sentences.note: "the federal district around the capital" is a gloss on the District of Columbia, carrying no figure.

sentences.text: In Metropolitan Railroad Company v. District of Columbia, the Supreme Court read it as making the District "a body corporate for municipal purposes", with power to make contracts and to sue and be sued, like any city.

assertions.text: In Metropolitan R. Co. v. District of Columbia the Supreme Court described the 1871 act as constituting the District "a body corporate for municipal purposes", with power to make contracts, sue and be sued.

quote.text: a body corporate for municipal purposes

sentences.text: The Court held that the District's "character as a mere municipal corporation has not been changed", and that the sovereign power over it is lodged "in the government of the United States", with Congress as its supreme legislature.

assertions.text: The Supreme Court held that the District's "character as a mere municipal corporation has not been changed".

quote.text: character as a mere municipal corporation has not been changed

assertions.text: The Supreme Court held that the sovereign power over the District is lodged "in the government of the United States", whose supreme legislative body is Congress.

quote.text: in the government of the United States

sentences.text: It even spelled out what that means for anyone charged with an offence there: "Crimes committed in the District are not crimes against the District, but against the United States".

assertions.text: The Supreme Court wrote: "Crimes committed in the District are not crimes against the District, but against the United States".

quote.text: Crimes committed in the District are not crimes against the District, but against the United States

sentences.text: Which leaves the biggest claim of all: that laws are contracts, and you can simply decline to sign.
In Indiana, a man who called himself a sovereign citizen sued the state, arguing that it could not tax him without a contract between them, and asked for a refund of $11.5 billion.

assertions.text: In Bey v. Indiana, the plaintiff argued that as a sovereign citizen he could not lawfully be taxed by Indiana without a contract, and sought an $11.5 billion refund.

sentences.text: The Seventh Circuit said it had "repeatedly rejected such claims", called the suit frivolous, and said he "was lucky to be spared sanctions for filing such a suit".

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit in Bey v. Indiana said it had "repeatedly rejected such claims" and called the suit frivolous.

quote.text: repeatedly rejected such claims

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit said the plaintiff "was lucky to be spared sanctions for filing such a suit".

quote.text: was lucky to be spared sanctions for filing such a suit

sentences.text: In New Zealand, a self-described freeman on the land appealed a traffic notice on the ground that he had never consented to the Land Transport Act, and the court struck out his claim as an abuse of process.

assertions.text: In James v The Corporation New Zealand Police, a freeman on the land who said he had not consented to the Land Transport Act had his claim struck out as an abuse of process.

sentences.text: Put the tricks side by side and the pattern is hard to miss.

Each real document says something narrower than the trick: a commercial-code rule about carrying on with a contract under protest, a fringe that the law gives no meaning, and an 1871 act that set up a municipal government for the District of Columbia.

assertions.text: UCC 1-308 governs continuing performance of a contract under a reservation of rights.
McCann v. Greenway found that flag fringe has no legal significance.
The Supreme Court read the 1871 act as making the District of Columbia a municipal corporation.

sentences.text: And in every ruling in this story, refusing consent, reserving your rights and calling statutes contracts got the same answer: the court had power over the person in front of it.

assertions.text: In Benabe, the Seventh Circuit held that a person claiming sovereign status is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts.
In State v. Smith, a defendant who reserved rights under UCC 1-308 and withheld consent was convicted.
In Bey v. Indiana and in a New Zealand freeman case, claims that a statute needed the person's contract or consent were rejected.

sentences.text: Researchers who reviewed pseudolaw in Australia and New Zealand put it flatly: "No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities".

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre write: "No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities".

quote.text: No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities

sentences.text: A history of these movements in Canada says Canadian courts "consistently rejected them", and the study of Supreme Court of Canada appeals concludes: "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit".

assertions.text: Netolitzky and Warman write: "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit".

qualifications: The sentence names the Supreme Court of Canada study.

sentences.text: In Queensland, an appeal court judge described one self-styled citizen sovereign's challenge to the police in a single line: "The argument was obvious nonsense and the magistrate rightly rejected it".

assertions.text: In Bradley v The Crown, the Queensland Court of Appeal wrote of the applicant's argument that a police officer had no power to charge him: "The argument was obvious nonsense and the magistrate rightly rejected it".

quote.text: The argument was obvious nonsense and the magistrate rightly rejected it

sentences.text: And back in Ohio, the appeals court noted that despite a wealth of material debunking them, "the claims continue to make their way to court and fail".

assertions.text: The Ohio appeals court in State v. Smith wrote that despite the wealth of information debunking them, "the claims continue to make their way to court and fail".

quote.text: the claims continue to make their way to court and fail

qualifications: The sentence names the court; the broad reviews are Canadian and Australasian, as the qualifications section says.

sentences.text: Does that mean these arguments have never worked anywhere, for anyone?

The evidence answers a narrower question: the broad reviews come from Canada, Australia and New Zealand, while in the United States we have a run of appeals courts saying they have rejected these theories again and again.

assertions.text: A review of pseudolaw in Australia and New Zealand reports that no courts accept these arguments.
A history of these ideas in Canada reports that Canadian courts consistently rejected them.
US appeals courts in Benabe and State v. Smith say they have repeatedly rejected sovereign-citizen theories.
qualifications: The sentence says the US record is a run of rulings, not a count.

sentences.note: The package has no US-wide count of outcomes; the sentence says the US record is a run of rulings, not a tally.

sentences.text: Even the Canadian record is incomplete, as one of its own authors points out: many of these proceedings never produce a reported judgment at all.

assertions.text: Netolitzky writes that many, if not most, OPCA proceedings do not result in a reported judgment.
qualifications: This sentence is itself the limitation on the written record.

sentences.text: The IRS says claims of being solely a citizen of a sovereign state, outside federal taxation, have been uniformly rejected by the courts, but it is writing about tax cases only.

assertions.text: The IRS says claims that individuals are solely citizens of a sovereign state and not subject to federal taxation have been uniformly rejected by the courts.
qualifications: The sentence says the IRS is writing about tax cases only.

sentences.text: Nothing in that record shows a jurisdiction trick that held up, though it cannot count unreported hearings or every American courtroom.
So what does that mean if you are the one standing in front of the judge?
First, the words buy you nothing: the man in Ohio reserved his rights and withheld his consent, and was convicted anyway.

assertions.text: The State v. Smith defendant reserved rights under UCC 1-308, withheld consent and was found guilty.

sentences.text: Second, they can cost you: in Benabe, the defendants kept interrupting after the judge had ruled, and the appeals court said they were "entering the territory of abuse of the judicial process".

assertions.text: In Benabe, the defendants continued to interrupt the trial after the court ruled, and the Seventh Circuit said they were "entering the territory of abuse of the judicial process".

quote.text: entering the territory of abuse of the judicial process

sentences.text: The Canadian history counts the price in plainer terms: "wasted court resources, unnecessary litigation expense, and sometimes devastating negative consequences to those who attempted to implement these schemes".

assertions.text: Netolitzky's history says these schemes have a social cost: "wasted court resources, unnecessary litigation expense, and sometimes devastating negative consequences to those who attempted to implement these schemes".

quote.text: wasted court resources, unnecessary litigation expense, and sometimes devastating negative consequences to those who attempted to implement these schemes

qualifications: The sentence calls it the Canadian history.

sentences.text: Say you get a ticket, and a video tells you the fix is a few words under your signature.
Whatever you write there, the court that hears the ticket gets its authority from the law, not from your signature.

assertions.text: Courts reject the claim that a person is outside their jurisdiction unless that person consents.

sentences.text: So when someone promises you a phrase that switches a court off, ask them for the ruling where it worked.
Back to the question we started with: is there anything you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's jurisdiction?
On the evidence here, no: not a reservation of rights under UCC 1-308, not a refusal to consent, not a fringed flag, not the act of 1871, and not the claim that laws are contracts.

assertions.text: Signing under UCC 1-308 does not take a person out of a court's jurisdiction.
Refusing consent does not put a person beyond a court's jurisdiction.
A fringed flag has no legal significance for a court's jurisdiction.
The 1871 act made the District of Columbia a municipal corporation, not the United States a private one.
Statutes bind people whether or not they consent to them as contracts.

sentences.text: Jurisdiction comes from law, not from what you sign or say in the room.

assertions.text: Courts hold that a person is subject to their jurisdiction regardless of consent or claimed status.
